glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
ulipur-munshibari.desc: The Munshi family's estate in Dharanibari union of Ulipur goes back to the mid-18th century, when Banwari Munshi, an official of the Nawab, was granted land here. The present mansion is believed to date from around 1880, going by an inscription, and was built by Binod Lal Munshi, an accountant of the Kasimbazar estate. Its facade is known for fine, richly decorated craftsmanship. The last family heads left for Kolkata after 1971, and the building has since passed into government hands. It is the main heritage stop on any Kurigram trip.
blocks: How to get there
From Kurigram town take a bus or CNG to Ulipur, then an auto or rickshaw to Munshibari in Dharanibari union.
Good to know
Try the famous Ulipur khirmohon in the bazar while you're in town. Don't climb on fragile parts of the building.

glance: Pabna Bhagyalakshmi Mishtanna Bhandar, Ulipur upazila town, Kurigram
ulipur-khirmohon.desc: Khirmohon is made from chhana, milk, ghee and a little flour, cooked with bay leaf and cardamom and served in thick syrup. In Ulipur the syrup itself is called kheer, which gives the sweet its name. It has been made here since the 1950s, and people come from other parts of the district just to eat it. Pabna Bhagyalakshmi Mishtanna Bhandar is the shop best known for it.

glance: Local hotels in Kurigram town and Chilmari; morning fish markets
kurigram-river-fish.desc: With so many rivers, fish is at the heart of Kurigram's kitchen. Korti, a small silvery fish, is a local favourite, alongside chela, boirali, and other catches from the Dharla and Brahmaputra. They are cooked simply, fried crisp or in a thin curry with tomato, onion and green chilli. Riverside markets in the morning are the best place to see the day's catch.
blocks: Good to know
Ask what came in that morning and have it fried.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
kotheshwar-shiva-temple.desc: Kotheshwar, in Gharialdanga union of Rajarhat upazila, is one of the oldest Hindu sites in the district. King Nilambar of Kamata is said to have founded a temple here in 1483, and on its ruins Rani Lakshmipriya of the Pangga estate built the present temple in 1897. Shiva is the main deity, and the goddess here is worshipped as Bhramari Devi. Shivaratri is the big night, when crowds keep vigil until dawn, and Durga Puja is also celebrated. On ordinary days it is a peaceful village temple.
blocks: How to get there
From Kurigram take a bus or CNG to Rajarhat, then an auto to Kotheshwar in Gharialdanga union.
Good to know
Visit on Shivaratri (February–March) to see it at its liveliest. Remove shoes before entering the shrine.

glance: Weekly char hats on the Brahmaputra, such as Jorgachh hat in Chilmari upazila
kurigram-charchom.desc: On the Brahmaputra chars of Kurigram, people keep buffaloes, and their thick milk makes a firmer, richer chhana than cow's milk. Char families turn it into chomchom at home, with a little flour, and sell it loose at the weekly char hats. Locals call it charchom, and you will not find it in town sweet shops. Because there is no shop rent or hired cook, it costs about half the price of a town sweet.
blocks: Good to know
Combine it with a boat trip from Chilmari; it is sold on hat days only.

glance: Roadside sellers in Kurigram town and near river ghats
char-bhutta.desc: On the dry-season chars of the Brahmaputra and Teesta, farmers grow maize where rice will not thrive. In spring, roadside sellers roast the cobs over charcoal until they blister, then rub them with salt, chilli and lime. It is a simple snack with a smoky, sweet flavour. Watching the harvest being ferried by boat from the chars adds to the experience.
blocks: Good to know
Choose cobs roasted in front of you.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
chandamari-mosque.desc: Chandamari Mondolpara Jame Mosque stands in Chandamari village, about 4 km south-west of Rajarhat upazila town. Archaeologists date it roughly to between 1584 and 1680, and its style mixes Sultanate features with Mughal design. The building is about 40 feet long and 20 feet wide, with three large domes, four corner minarets and sixteen small domes around the roof. Three mihrabs line the inside, and a big pond lies in front. It is still in daily use.
blocks: How to get there
From Kurigram take a bus or CNG to Rajarhat, then an auto about 4 km south-west to Chandamari.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid prayer times. Mekurtari Shahi Mosque and Kotheshwar temple are in the same upazila.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
chilmari-river-port.desc: Chilmari has been a river port on the Brahmaputra for centuries, and its name lives on in the famous Bhawaiya song about a bullock-cart driver heading to Chilmari bondor. From the Ramna ghat area, boats carry people and goods to the chars and across to Roumari and Rajibpur. The scale of the river here, often several kilometres wide, is impressive. In the dry season, sandbanks stretch to the horizon.
blocks: How to get there
Buses run from Kurigram town to Chilmari (about 1 hour); then a rickshaw to the ghat.
Good to know
Hire boats only from the main ghat and agree on the fare first. Carry water and sun protection.

glance: About 20 BDT for a chomchom, 40–50 BDT for sandesh or khirmohon (2023)
Jhontu Mistanna Bhandar, Kalibari area, Kurigram town
jhontu-mistanna-bhandar.desc: Jhontu Mistanna Bhandar started in 1939 and is still a small tin-roofed shop among concrete buildings in the Kalibari area of Kurigram town. Everyone in town knows it by name. Its chomchom and round white sweets are the everyday favourites, and it also makes khirmohon, rasmanjuri and chhanar sandesh. The family has kept the old recipes and the old care over quality.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
dharla-riverfront.desc: The Dharla flows past Kurigram town, and the bridge across it has become the town's favourite spot to watch the river. In winter the water runs clear and shallow, with sandbanks and grazing cattle, while in the monsoon it swells fast and brown. Fishermen cast nets from small boats, and tea stalls line the embankment. It is a relaxed place to see daily river life.
blocks: How to get there
A short auto-rickshaw ride from Kurigram town centre.
Good to know
Late afternoon is best. Avoid boat trips when the river is in flood.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
naodanga-zamindar-bari.desc: Naodanga, in Phulbari upazila, was the seat of the Bakshi zamindars, founded by Pramod Ranjan Bakshi, who received the title Bahadur from the British. Their estate covered much of present Phulbari. The rest of the family moved to Cooch Behar, and the last zamindar, Bisheshwar Prasad Bakshi, followed after zamindari was abolished. What remains of the house now stands among trees, and a goddess temple on the grounds is still in use. Few visitors come.
blocks: How to get there
From Kurigram cross the Dharla Bridge to Phulbari by bus or CNG, then an auto to Naodanga union.
Good to know
Ask locals for the 'jomidar bari'. Go in daylight; the grounds are overgrown.

kurigram-bhawaiya.desc: Bhawaiya is the folk music of the greater Rangpur region and neighbouring parts of India, recognisable by its distinctive breaks and quivers in the voice. Songs tell of bullock-cart drivers, boatmen, lovers waiting by the river and the hardships of rural life. The dotara, a plucked string instrument, provides the main accompaniment. Kurigram has a strong tradition of Bhawaiya singers, and the songs are performed at fairs, cultural events and family gatherings.
blocks: Good to know
Ask at the district Shilpakala Academy or at local fairs about performances.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
bhawaiya-museum-ulipur.desc: In Ulipur upazila, a community museum preserves nearly two thousand everyday rural objects, from farm tools and household items to musical instruments linked with Bhawaiya. Many of the pieces have disappeared from village life, and the collection keeps their memory alive. It is modest, run with limited resources, and few outsiders know about it. A visit gives context to the songs you will hear in the region.
blocks: How to get there
Ulipur is between Kurigram town and Chilmari; ask locally for the Bhawaiya museum.
Good to know
Opening is informal; ask around in Ulipur or call ahead through local contacts.

mekurtari-shahi-mosque.desc: Mekurtari Shahi Mosque stands in Byaparipara village, about 1 km north-east of Rajarhat upazila town. With no inscription, its date is uncertain, but its Mughal-style design suggests it is a couple of centuries old. Local tradition says it was built by a village landowner, Chhamir Uddin Byapari, after he returned from walking all the way to Hajj. The narrow building, about 32 feet by 10, carries three large domes, four tall corner minarets and eight smaller ones, behind a low wall and a decorative gateway. It is a protected monument that few outsiders know.
blocks: How to get there
From Rajarhat upazila town, it is a short rickshaw or auto ride north-east to Byaparipara.
Good to know
Combine with Chandamari Mosque and Kotheshwar temple for a half-day in Rajarhat. Dress modestly.

glance: 345 km to Kurigram by road, 9–11 hours by bus or car
sonahat-bridge.desc: In Bhurungamari upazila, an old steel bridge built for a colonial-era railway crosses the Dudhkumar River. The railway is long gone, and a newer road bridge now runs nearby, leading to the Sonahat land port on the Indian border. The river is wide and clear in winter, with views of fields and border villages. It is a quiet, scenic stop in the far north.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus from Kurigram to Bhurungamari, then an auto-rickshaw to Sonahat.
Good to know
It is close to the border; carry ID.
